Foundation in the iOS 26.0.1 shared cache

Target: iPhone 11 (iPhone12,1), iOS 26.0.1 (23A355), arm64e.

Observed

  • The official FileSystem image contains /System/Library/Frameworks/Foundation.framework as a directory, but no regular file at /System/Library/Frameworks/Foundation.framework/Foundation.
  • The SystemOS dyld shared cache lists that latter path as an in-cache image. Its UUID is 0555AF54-2075-3F2D-BC40-733E55EEE95A, and the cache UUID is C0A7E671-35E1-3E6C-842D-FCE4E0A08C7E.
  • ipsw dyld macho <cache> /System/Library/Frameworks/Foundation.framework/Foundation --json --loads reports DylibInCache in the Mach-O flags. Its load commands include reexports of /usr/lib/libobjc.A.dylib and /System/Library/Frameworks/CoreFoundation.framework/CoreFoundation.

Interpretation

The framework bundle path and the executable image are different catalog objects. A filesystem-only explorer would show the bundle while missing its executable code; a cache-only explorer would miss the resources in the bundle. The Atlas links both under the same logical install name without inventing an on-disk executable.

The Foundation.framework directory in the Atlas ↗ shows its observed resource files and the logical Foundation cache image in separate sections.

The Foundation method-surface note ↗ traces 11,045 Objective-C method entries back to this same cache image and its exact build.

This is a static observation of the official firmware. It does not establish which Foundation methods a particular process executes at runtime.

Reproduce

The published indexes are `filesystem.json.gz` ↗ and `dyld.json` ↗. The extraction command, exact firmware hash, and tool version are recorded in the acquisition notes ↗. The source IPSW and full cache stay local.
research.summary: The framework bundle exists in the FileSystem image, while its executable image is indexed inside the SystemOS dyld shared cache.

How much of Foundation's Objective-C method surface is indexed?

Target: iPhone 11 (iPhone12,1), iOS 26.0.1 (23A355). Source: official restore IPSW SHA-256 2773217713e94b81fbbaa6ecb6b7e87fb176f58f5edefdb868d8d71ec6547bd2, iOS arm64e dyld cache family UUID C0A7E671-35E1-3E6C-842D-FCE4E0A08C7E. The inspected image is /System/Library/Frameworks/Foundation.framework/Foundation, Mach-O UUID 0555AF54-2075-3F2D-BC40-733E55EEE95A.

Observed coverage

  • A complete ipsw class-dump --re -V of this image reports 720 class declarations and 53 categories. Its table of contents reports 62 protocol entries, while the output renders 48 @protocol declarations. The full local dump has SHA-256 fb73e704e1718d670886de80c7e86142d1dadd4ff5b7ef6190f45c0da6de0fd0; it is not published. The table and rendered counts are recorded separately because this source does not explain their difference.
  • The derived method catalog ↗ contains 11,045 method entries: 10,215 under classes and 830 under categories. Each entry has a selector, class or category label, and implementation address inside this exact image's __TEXT segment. The catalog preserves class and category boundaries. No group contains a duplicate selector and method kind in this dump.
  • All 720 class names and metadata addresses match the separate dyld Objective-C optimization table ↗ for this image. All 53 category metadata addresses lie in the image's mapped segments. The extracted analysis derivative has SHA-256 078c2898a74339d91c8a032d7f735fa4770aed75dcb69e5d3bed9a64d0c49afc; it is not an on-device standalone executable.
  • Protocol declarations are excluded from the implementation-address count. A protocol declaration is an interface record, not evidence of an implementation in this image.

How to use it

The Objective-C methods view ↗ lists the indexed images. Choose Foundation to search class names, category labels, selectors, and implementation addresses. The site loads its compressed method bucket only after selection. The Foundation filesystem view ↗ separately shows the framework's on-disk resources and its logical in-cache executable.

This count covers one cache image in one build. It does not cover every image in the iOS cache, methods dynamically added at runtime, generated subclasses, or method bodies. A selector and address do not prove that a process called the method; selecting a tweak hook requires function-body and runtime evidence.

Reproduce

Follow the acquisition record ↗ to obtain the exact IPSW and intact cache family. Keep the full dump and extracted analysis derivative under ignored .local storage:

ipsw class-dump <MAIN_DSC> /System/Library/Frameworks/Foundation.framework/Foundation --re -V --no-color > .local/rea/foundation-all-classes.txt

ipsw dyld extract <MAIN_DSC> /System/Library/Frameworks/Foundation.framework/Foundation --output .local/rea/extracted --slide --objc --stubs --cache <MAIN_DSC>.a2s

python3 tools/catalog_objc_image_methods.py --class-dump .local/rea/foundation-all-classes.txt --image .local/rea/extracted/Foundation --image-sha256 078c2898a74339d91c8a032d7f735fa4770aed75dcb69e5d3bed9a64d0c49afc --install-name /System/Library/Frameworks/Foundation.framework/Foundation --segments catalog/ios/23A355/dyld-segments.json --objc-classes catalog/ios/23A355/objc-classes.json --expected-method-count 11045 --output catalog/ios/23A355/objc-image-methods-Foundation.json.gz

The generator checks the derivative hash and UUID, source-build identities, class-table equality, class and category counts, protocol count bounds, and every implementation address. The website builder repeats the catalog consistency and address checks before publishing derived metadata.

What does the per-image Objective-C method catalog cover?

Target: iPhone 11 (iPhone12,1), iOS 26.0.1 (23A355). Source: official restore IPSW SHA-256 2773217713e94b81fbbaa6ecb6b7e87fb176f58f5edefdb868d8d71ec6547bd2, iOS arm64e cache family UUID C0A7E671-35E1-3E6C-842D-FCE4E0A08C7E. See the acquisition record ↗.

Horizontal coverage

  • The method explorer ↗ has a separate catalog for all 4,170 iOS cache images. Together they contain 3,065,801 Objective-C method entries, 217,455 rendered class declarations, and 10,623 categories. Choose an image to load its compressed method bucket. The image explorer ↗ gives each library a short, source-derived overview and a direct method link.
  • 1,014 images have zero listed methods. For 406 of these, ipsw class-dump --re -V succeeded but emitted an empty file. These are recorded as inspected zero-result dumps with the empty file's SHA-256; a zero is not evidence that an image has no code or no Swift or C functions.
  • The dyld Objective-C optimization class table lists classes in 3,443 of the 4,170 images. We also scanned the other 727. Sixteen of them contain 119 method entries in their class dumps, so class-table absence was not treated as method absence.
  • The catalogs retain 565 Swift-marked class declarations absent from the optimization class table and one category for which the dump omits the class name. Ten method entries have no decoded selector and remain explicitly unknown. Raw selectors with unusual punctuation remain as printed. Full dump UTF-8 decoding produced 424 replacement characters, recorded per image rather than hidden.

Source checks and meaning

Each catalog records the exact install name, image UUID, full class-dump SHA-256, classes, categories, selectors where decoded, and IMP addresses. Class identities are checked against the separate dyld optimization table; extra class declarations must be marked Swift. Class and category counts are checked against the dump's table of contents when present. Every IMP is checked against the defining image's __TEXT range from the independently collected Mach-O segment catalog. The site builder repeats these checks and rejects duplicate install names.

The first 69 catalogs were made with extracted Mach-O analysis derivatives; each records that derivative's SHA-256 and had its UUID checked against the intact cache. The other 4,101 were generated directly from the intact cache. Before each direct-cache batch, the collector verified all 80 cache-family files against the official firmware catalog by SHA-256; each new catalog also records the verified main-cache hash. An extracted image hash is therefore absent from those catalogs. Raw dumps, cache bytes, and extracted Apple binaries stay local; Git contains only compressed derived metadata.

An entry describes static metadata in this one firmware build. It does not show which process loaded an image, which method ran, or which duplicate implementation wins at runtime. The overview names prominent method groups as clues, not a verified behavioral description. Foundation ↗ and SpringBoard ↗ provide examples of deeper notes. The research TODO ↗ tracks later function-body and runtime studies.

Reproduce or extend

With the exact local cache family, run:

python3 tools/batch_objc_image_methods.py --cache .local/cache/23A355__iPhone12,1/dyld_shared_cache_arm64e --cache-only --dyld-catalog catalog/ios/23A355/dyld.json --segments catalog/ios/23A355/dyld-segments.json --objc-classes catalog/ios/23A355/objc-classes.json --output-dir catalog/ios/23A355 --workdir .local/rea/batch --all-images --limit 100

The batch skips existing catalogs after checking their source identity. --include selects an exact install name for review. Run python3 tools/build_site.py to validate and rebuild the public site. The collector also supports extracted-image mode with --a2s for focused work.

Which named code symbols are visible in the iOS shared cache?

Target: all 4,170 logical images in the intact arm64e iOS dyld shared-cache family from the official iPhone 11 iOS 26.0.1 (23A355) IPSW, SHA-256 2773217713e94b81fbbaa6ecb6b7e87fb176f58f5edefdb868d8d71ec6547bd2. Cache family UUID: C0A7E671-35E1-3E6C-842D-FCE4E0A08C7E. This excludes the separate DriverKit cache and physical Mach-O files outside the cache.

An ipsw 3.1.739 pass with dyld macho --symbols --demangle yielded 6,585,655 unique named `__text` symbol records in 3,798 images. The other 372 images had no matching named record. The raw output contained 577,724 additional duplicate rows with identical address, name, visibility, and segment; the catalog counts them without repeating them in the browser. Of the unique records, 2,734,567 have the textual shape of an Objective-C method (-[Class selector] or +[Class selector]). This is a name-pattern count, not a verified subset of the separate 3,065,801-entry Objective-C method catalog ↗, and the two totals must not be added as if they were disjoint functions.

Every physical member of the 80-file cache family was checked by size and complete SHA-256 against the official IPSW inventory before collection. Each image's Mach-O UUID was checked against that inventory. Every published symbol address falls inside an executable segment's __text section for that exact image. The catalog keeps the SHA-256 of each raw symbol dump and Mach-O table of contents, along with counts of duplicate, unnamed, out-of-section, and undecodable rows. In this pass the latter three counts are zero. Raw command output and resumable checkpoints stay outside Git.

The shared-cache image explorer ↗ shows the symbol count for each image. Selecting Browse named `__text` symbols loads one of 128 compressed buckets; the list can be searched by name, address, visibility, or segment. Foundation has 39,492 named records, of which 10,663 match the Objective-C name pattern. SpringBoard.framework has 69,889 named records, of which 53,010 match that pattern. The site keeps the symbol list beside, rather than inside, the separate Objective-C method view.

A symbol-table name can denote a private implementation detail, alias, compiler-generated label, or other code-section label. Stripping may remove names while leaving code. This index is a horizontal map of visible names, not a complete function list, public API list, description of implementation, runtime trace, or verified tweak hook. Functional introductions for documented framework families are tracked separately in the framework coverage note ↗; per-library implementation questions remain on the research TODO ↗.

The aggregate source is `ios-cache-symbols.json.gz` ↗. To regenerate it from the exact locally extracted cache:

python3 tools/catalog_ios_cache_symbols.py --cache-main .local/cache/23A355__iPhone12,1/dyld_shared_cache_arm64e --dyld-catalog catalog/ios/23A355/dyld.json --workdir .local/ios-cache-symbol-work --output catalog/ios/23A355/ios-cache-symbols.json.gz --workers 8

How many cached frameworks have a sourced introduction?

The official iPhone 11 iOS 26.0.1 (23A355) cache contains 4,170 logical iOS images. Of these, 227 have an exact top-level path of the form /System/Library/Frameworks/Name.framework/Name with a non-underscore-prefixed name. This path pattern defines the scope of this pass; it is not a claim that every framework exposes an iPhone developer API.

The introduction catalog ↗ now links 221 of those 227 images to Apple Developer source material. Every entry records the exact install name, a short description, the page URL, the SHA-256 of the retrieved source document, and the check date. 178 descriptions are clearly marked short verbatim excerpts of at most 25 words; the others are authored summaries. The separate DriverKit cache has one additional sourced introduction, for 222 catalog entries total.

Earlier additions use MetricKit ↗, MusicKit ↗, and OpenGL ES ↗ framework pages; the IdentityLookupUI view-controller page ↗, whose framework landing page has no substantive abstract; and Apple's archived iOS Core Audio guide ↗ for OpenAL. These describe documented API families or types, not the runtime behavior of the exact cached images. A new MobileCoreServices introduction cites Apple’s archived iOS Uniform Type Identifiers guide ↗, which places legacy UTI constants and utility functions in that framework. The Metal Performance Primitives guide ↗ explains Metal 4 tensor operations on M5; its introduction explicitly does not establish that the iPhone 11 can run those APIs merely because an image is present in this cache.

The BusinessChat entry links Apple's Messages for Business overview ↗ to the service context while explicitly stating that the page does not document the exact cache binary. The exact-image study ↗ provides separate static evidence for its named classes and methods.

The remaining six top-level names are CoreServices, RealityFoundation, StickerFoundation, StickerKit, SwiftUICore, and Twitter. These are missing sourced introductions, not absent cache images or proof that no documentation exists elsewhere. The direct Apple framework Markdown paths did not provide usable introductions for them in this pass.

All six now have separate first-pass exact-cache notes in the Research view: CoreServices ↗, RealityFoundation ↗, StickerFoundation ↗, StickerKit ↗, SwiftUICore ↗, and Twitter ↗. Those notes distinguish visible metadata, bounded role inferences, and unknown runtime behavior. They do not replace a primary-source description of each image's implementation.

The shared-cache image explorer ↗ offers Browse introductions and the intro: search prefix. A documentation page describes a documented API family or type, not the exact implementation, the complete method surface of the 23A355 binary, runtime loading, or whether a particular API is public on this iPhone. All 4,170 images still have a separate source-derived metadata overview and an Objective-C method result. Other private frameworks, libraries, support components, and the six names above remain in the research TODO ↗ for functional investigation with suitable primary evidence.
research.summary: Apple Developer sources now supply linked introductions for 221 of 227 exact top-level framework images. Other cache images retain metadata overviews while functional research continues.

What does the BusinessChat cache image expose?

Target: the iPhone 11 iOS 26.0.1 build 23A355 iOS dyld cache, UUID C0A7E671-35E1-3E6C-842D-FCE4E0A08C7E. The exact BusinessChat image is /System/Library/Frameworks/BusinessChat.framework/BusinessChat, UUID 7682AB26-7957-39CA-B847-062728936E02. The intact main cache has SHA-256 6097e3ce9e29cfccd19d5aab182d006868a93a14c3a5cebcb22b6675c1527b19; the full 80-file iOS cache family was separately matched against this phone by device-side SHA-256. The static evidence below does not establish that a process loaded this image.

First-pass role

The exact-image method catalog ↗ records 270 Objective-C methods across 34 classes and one category. Named classes include BCChatButton, BCWebViewController, BCMessage, BCMessageInfo, BCAuthenticationManager, and several BCOAuth2* request and response types. The symbol catalog ↗ records 316 named __text symbols. The load-command catalog ↗ records 17 direct library loads, including BusinessChatService, Accounts, UIKit, WebKit, AuthKit, and Security. These names and declarations suggest a business-chat user interface and an authentication path; they do not prove a complete workflow.

An ipsw dyld extract derivative of this exact cache image has SHA-256 4cfd1b7be0564417aa9dafbd14c3639698cec4651fa4107c9f872ec0af1ab636. Its file hash is an analysis derivative, not the device's cache hash. Hopper through REA recovered -[BCChatButton setup] at 0x234d181a8. The pseudocode references localized CHAT_BUTTON_DOUBLE_LINE_* and accessibility-label keys, a MessagesIcon image, fonts, subviews, and updateAppearanceForState:. This supports the narrow inference that the class builds a chat button UI. It does not establish where the button appears or whether it appeared on this phone.

The same image names -[BCAuthenticationManager fetchTokenWithRequest:completion:] at 0x234d1ad8c, processQueryItems:completion: at 0x234d1b3dc, and exchangeCode:completion: at 0x234d1b604. The inspected fetchTokenWithRequest:completion: pseudocode reads the request URL and its query items and conditionally calls processQueryItems:completion:. This supports an authentication-flow hypothesis. The inspected portion does not prove an outgoing network request, a successful token exchange, or runtime use.

Evidence and next questions

The local REA evidence bundle is kept outside Git at .local/rea/businesschat-evidence.json. Relevant retained IDs are ev_5c22b7ba3bd8f6e69e60c112ac6a4ae4b2bcce420c73f20c8fdc36258c72a62c (class labels), ev_2dd8e1872a8c451a7c82ede688f9d2a2e392ccc1f2bd44e69faf18a49470bd (chat-button methods), ev_6157f44f054c528f22e7777214331dc5364a35519826b6303bee84b167744a4c (button setup pseudocode), and ev_de6deb2fe7bcc016fdc20c4f321e07fd53ee3122ed05b865e5ed86b7cde1a6f9 (token-request pseudocode). REA used Hopper for the focused analysis; Ghidra's class-label query failed with a 2 GB Java heap limit and contributed no negative finding.

Reproduce the derivative with ipsw dyld extract <MAIN_DSC> /System/Library/Frameworks/BusinessChat.framework/BusinessChat --output <PRIVATE_DIR> --slide --objc --stubs --cache <MAIN_DSC>.a2s, then check its SHA-256 and the addresses above. The acquisition record ↗ identifies the complete cache family and firmware source. Next work is to follow BCChatAction and BCNetworkProvider call sites, identify which process loads the image, and confirm any proposed hook point on the device before treating it as a tweak target.
research.summary: The exact cache image exposes 270 Objective-C methods, including chat-button and authentication code. Focused static analysis supports a chat UI role; runtime ownership and the complete workflow remain open.

These names and the service's declared load suggest an update orchestration role. Service entry and message dispatch

A focused Ghidra 12.1.4 pass over the two device-acquired binaries found that the service executable's entry at 0x100000698 is one b instruction to its _update_brain_service_main import stub at 0x10000069c. The stub loads a pointer and branches to it. Its import is named @rpath/UpdateBrainLibrary.dylib::_update_brain_service_main; the service has no local update workflow to describe beyond that handoff. This is a static import and branch, not a confirmed dyld resolution or process launch.

The library defines _update_brain_service_main at 0x37c9c (analyzed body through 0x380fb). The recovered call sequence opens a restore log, prepares a queue and three signal sources, installs logging and partition callbacks, probes media, calls MSUBrainServerImpl::startListener: at 0x2fca4, and enters xpc_main with _UpdateBrainService_event_handler at 0x381c8. The listener method creates an anonymous NSXPCListener, sets its delegate and queue, and resumes it. These are code paths visible in the binary; their effects on this phone have not been observed.

For an incoming connection, the handler sets an event block and target queue, then resumes the XPC connection. The queued block at 0x387ac reads the Command key from a dictionary and passes the message to _handle_message at 0x44130. That function reads CommandParameters, searches a seven-entry command table at 0x34d840 (seven 24-byte records), calls _msu_client_is_entitled at 0x44304, and only then invokes the selected handler through a function pointer. The entitlement helper checks for a Boolean XPC entitlement value and returns false when it is absent, false, or not Boolean. An unknown command or failed entitlement leads to an error reply in the recovered control flow. Ghidra did not resolve the indirect handler call as a normal callee edge; the table mapping below comes from its initialized bytes and string records.

  • PreflightUpdate → _handle_MSUPreflightUpdate at 0x38be8.
  • PrepareUpdate → _handle_MSUPrepareUpdate at 0x3941c.
  • ApplyUpdate → _handle_MSUApplyUpdate at 0x3963c.
  • SuspendUpdate → _handle_MSUSuspendUpdate at 0x39744.
  • ResumeUpdate → _handle_MSUResumeUpdate at 0x397d8.
  • PingService → _handle_MSUPingService at 0x3984c.
  • CommitStash → _handle_MSUCommitStash at 0x39a8c.

Six entries carry the allow-softwareupdated entitlement string. PingService carries com.apple.private.softwareupdated-helpers. The comparison in _handle_message uses strncmp with the table command's length; whether a longer request string is accepted as a command, and how any client constructs requests, remain untested. A command name or handler address does not establish that a client invoked it, that an update ran, or that the handler is a safe tweak point.

Target: the connected iPhone 11 (iPhone12,1) on iOS 26.0.1 (23A355). A read-only follow-up on 2026-11-06 UTC scanned the Data and Mobile data mount views separately. Their private snapshot manifest has SHA-256 7a5e8ed0996521bd534af8561e5ed36fa98e6b2ec73be34529096e076e76a5d1. These are partial views: find encountered the same 16 and 57 protected directories as the earlier snapshot, with no overlap between the two error sets. All 73 errors were Operation not permitted. A separate read-only stat attempt also returned Operation not permitted for every one of those directory paths. The underlying protection mechanism and descendant counts are unknown. No protected directory was bypassed.

A later bounded root-SSH probe checked all 73 of those exact paths without listing their contents. Every parent directory's metadata was readable (70 parents had mode 755, two 777, one 700), while stat on every target and find -maxdepth 0 on every target failed. A further read-only stat sample of ten target directories as the mobile account also failed for all ten. The result rules out a missing or unreadable parent as a general explanation; it does not identify the mechanism enforcing the denial. The aggregate probe is kept privately at .local/live-device-data-followup-20261106/protected-access-probe.json. iCTRL's port 8200 was not listening at that observation time, and notifyutil was absent from the device shell, so those passes could not check lock state. The owner subsequently confirmed that the phone was already unlocked; a fresh root-SSH sample still returned Operation not permitted for ten protected targets. The earlier lock-state explanation is no longer a useful working assumption.

The root shell reported UID 0, platform-application = true, and com.apple.private.security.no-sandbox = true. It could stat /rootfs and /rootfs/private/var, but could not stat the ten protected targets. Apple's Data Vault documentation ↗ describes entitlement-gated filesystem access, and Apple Platform Security ↗ says this protection is enforced independently of the app sandbox. These sources make Data Vault a candidate explanation, not an identified cause for these paths. An Apple DTS explanation ↗ also cautions that the UF_DATAVAULT file flag is not a universal detector.

A temporary, signed, read-only getattrlist/getattrlistbulk probe was calibrated before interpreting flags. The SSH shell could see an ordinary /rootfs/private/var control path, but the probe returned ENOENT for that same path and all 73 protected targets; it therefore had a different effective path view and cannot establish whether any target has `UF_DATAVAULT`. Adding platform and no-sandbox entitlement keys to the temporary probe did not change that result. RootHide's path documentation ↗ describes /rootfs as the bootstrap view of the original iOS root, while its vroot documentation ↗ describes compile-time path API replacement. This offers a plausible explanation for the ad hoc probe's ENOENT; the observation alone does not identify its exact runtime setup. The original aggregate and invalid-for-flag-inference calibration are kept privately at .local/live-device-data-followup-20261106/protected-flags-probe.json.

A follow-up on 2026-11-06 UTC used native /private/var paths in the same probe. Ordinary /tmp, /private/var, and the Mobile Library parent all returned metadata and flags successfully. All 73 protected targets then returned EPERM from direct getattrlist; each parent directory opened, and getattrlistbulk found the target name but did not return its flags. By contrast, the same probe still got ENOENT for the /rootfs spelling of the control and target paths. This establishes that the 73 direct denials persist after correcting the probe's path view. It does not identify Data Vault or reveal UF_DATAVAULT: no target flag was observed, and Apple cautions that the flag would not be a universal detector even if available. The private aggregate, control cases, and exact source-error digest are saved at .local/live-device-data-followup-20261106/roothide-physical-path-probe.json. The temporary executable and directory were removed after each run. No protected directory was bypassed; its descendants remain unknown.

  • Data: The later snapshot and type pass had exactly the same 23,490 unique reachable regular-file paths. Of these, 303 descriptions contained a Mach-O signature: 179 executables, 112 dylibs, 7 bundles, and 5 dSYM companion files. All candidates are within private app-bundle storage; no path or binary is public.
  • Mobile data: The snapshot and type pass each saw 29,500 unique paths, but 34 paths appeared and 34 disappeared between passes. With the same pinned root SSH route, a later read-only sha256sum -z pass hashed all 303 Data and 3 Mobile data candidate paths. A subsequent read-only tar transfer acquired all 306 candidate files into ignored .local. Every local SHA-256 matched its earlier device-side hash, and all acquired sizes still matched the private snapshot sizes. The transfer exited zero; no candidate was missing, changed, or truncated. Its local archive reader accepted only requested regular-file members and stored files under opaque private names rather than mirroring app paths. The private acquisition manifest has SHA-256 28493cdab9ea4b22c3200dc3f560b947f867e94db6739dcef82a07b6ecd7de3d, referencing the private hash manifest above. Raw transfer diagnostics remain private.

Data accounts for 303 files and 307 slices; Mobile data accounts for 3 files and 5 slices. Five Data files are dSYM companions rather than ordinary launchable code. This verifies the reachable candidates from those type passes, not every possible code-bearing file in either partial mount: 73 protected directories remain unreadable, Mobile data changed between metadata passes, and scripts or embedded formats were outside the type filter. No private path, individual file hash, UUID, or binary is published.

Private static metadata pass

The 306 byte-verified files were hard-linked into an ignored, permission-restricted .local analysis tree and rechecked against device-side SHA-256 values. Existing Mach-O analyzers then checked all 312 slices for direct library loads, named __text symbols, Swift dump metadata, and embedded signing structures. The private aggregate validator checked each result against the exact file hash, architecture, and UUID in the acquisition manifest. Only the counts below are published; individual app paths, method names, symbols, dependency names, entitlements, and signing identities remain private.

  • Data: 303 files and 307 slices. Objective-C: 281 parsed with 226,114 methods, 14 no info, three failed, and five dSYM not applicable. Other static results: 10,243 direct loads, 146,366 named __text symbols, 107,258 Swift declarations, and 302 CodeDirectories.
  • Mobile data: Three files and five slices. Objective-C: two parsed with 13 methods and one no-info result. Other static results: 18 direct loads, eight named __text symbols, no Swift declarations, and five CodeDirectories.

The three Objective-C failures all have LC_ENCRYPTION_INFO_64 with crypt_id=1, and each encrypted file range overlaps at least one __objc_* section. Two class dumps returned read errors; the third exited zero but emitted malformed, nonprintable interface data. This is an on-disk encryption limit, not evidence of zero methods. Their method counts remain unknown. The private failure evidence JSON has SHA-256 043d15fa38f23ce185ea7781de1e769fe210dbd2d9ed13171b0353bdb3a4e1bf; no decrypted memory or runtime behavior was inspected. The five dSYM companions are debug-symbol files and were not treated as Objective-C code images. Across both mounts, 105 files yielded no named __text symbols; 83 slices reported no Swift information, 39 Swift dumps were partially parsed, and two slices had Swift sections the dumper could not parse. Five slices had no embedded signature; 307 had a parseable CodeDirectory. These are static metadata results, not proof of runtime loading, signature trust, or a complete callable surface.

The private aggregate is saved at .local/live-device-data-followup-20261106/analysis-full/aggregate-summary.json. Its validator is `tools/summarize_private_data_macho_analysis.py` ↗; the input hard-link preparation is `tools/prepare_private_data_macho_analysis.py` ↗. Neither the private aggregate nor per-file analysis outputs are site data. Protected directories, Mobile data churn, scripts, and embedded formats remain outside this pass.

Reproduce and next work

With the saved, pinned root SSH route to this exact phone, make a private metadata snapshot of each mount and run find <MOUNT> -xdev -type f -exec file -0 -0 -- {} + without crossing mount boundaries. Preserve NUL-delimited results and stderr privately. Compare each emitted path set with its snapshot, count descriptions containing Mach-O or universal binary, and treat every inaccessible directory and changed path as an explicit limit. The collection procedure ↗ explains the private snapshot format; the public mount catalog ↗ retains the earlier observation's counts.

The private hash and acquisition procedures ↗ validate the saved snapshot, NUL-delimited type results, exact device build, tar members, and local byte identity without printing private paths. The private metadata pass adds broad static interface and dependency counts; deeper per-library work should select reviewed system components rather than expose app-specific details. A cause for the 73 access denials requires separate evidence. Script and embedded-code formats remain outside this Mach-O type pass.

The RootHide SSH namespace exposes the base system at /rootfs and a separate jailbreak installation tree at /. The collection procedure ↗ records the mount mapping and the two protected data-volume gaps.

GNU file identified 464 Mach-O files in that jailbreak tree. A device-side SHA-256 pass covered all 464. The same 464 paths were copied into a private local archive; every extracted file matched its device-side hash. A bounded Mach-O header and load-command parser then read all files without an error. A .dylib filename count would miss shared-library slices inside other containers.

  • Hash and UUID identify these acquired bytes at the observation time; the device may change after collection.
  • An exact-file class dump covers all 463 published files. It found 4,781 static Objective-C method entries in 61 files; 402 files reported no ObjC information. Mach-O load commands across all 493 slices declare 3,070 direct dylib loads and 572 runpaths. Named symbols, Swift declarations, code-signing identities, and actual dyld resolution remain unindexed for this live set.
  • The data-volume scan was partial because of protected directories. This note does not claim every possible executable on the phone was readable.

What Swift metadata is visible in standalone Mach-O files?

Target: all 3,363 physical Mach-O files in the FileSystem, SystemOS, and AppOS images of the official iPhone 11 iOS 26.0.1 (23A355) IPSW, SHA-256 2773217713e94b81fbbaa6ecb6b7e87fb176f58f5edefdb868d8d71ec6547bd2. The file inventory ↗ separates these physical files from images in the dyld shared cache.

An exact-file ipsw swift-dump pass reported 282,145 type, protocol, and extension declaration lines and 294,746 method or protocol-requirement lines. The latter include 224,323 lines explicitly marked <stripped> by the tool. These are dump rows, not reconstructed Swift source or a count of unique in-file definitions. The tool reported no Swift information for 2,068 files. Of the 1,295 files with Swift sections, 1,162 parsed without malformed lines and 133 had partial text parsing. Fifty-one of those 1,162 produced no declaration rows despite having Swift sections.

The partial outputs contain 2,122 omitted lines with unexpected structure or undecodable content; 1,171 Unicode replacement characters appeared across raw dumps. Those files remain labeled partially_parsed in the catalog and site. A malformed line can interrupt a larger declaration, so the visible row count for those files is a lower bound on what this tool might recover. A zero row count is not proof of no Swift code or methods. Protocol names can also be references rather than types defined by that file.

Every mounted file was checked against the standalone inventory by size and full SHA-256 before the dump. Its Mach-O UUID was checked against the inventory, and Swift section names, addresses, and sizes were recorded from the load commands. Raw tool output remains local; each public file record includes its SHA-256. The Standalone Mach-O explorer ↗ shows the per-file status and loads a compressed type/member bucket only when opened. For example, the physical Shortcuts executable has searchable Swift declaration and member lines, while /usr/lib/dyld reports no Swift information.

This pass complements the Objective-C method ↗ and named code symbol ↗ indexes. None of the three alone is a complete function inventory, and static metadata does not establish runtime calls, public API, or safe tweak hooks. The iOS cache's Swift conformance catalog ↗ is a separate source with different records.

The aggregate catalog is `standalone-swift.json.gz` ↗. To regenerate it with the exact mounted images:

python3 tools/catalog_standalone_swift.py --macho-catalog catalog/ios/23A355/standalone-macho.json.gz --filesystem-root .local/mount-fs --systemos-root .local/mount-sys --appos-root .local/mount-app --workdir .local/standalone-swift-work --output catalog/ios/23A355/standalone-swift.json.gz --workers 4
research.summary: All 3,363 exact standalone files were checked: 1,295 have Swift sections, yielding 282,145 declaration and 294,746 member or requirement lines. 133 outputs are explicitly partial.

Two kernelcache variants in the iPhone 11 restore IPSW

Target: iPhone 11 (iPhone12,1), iOS 26.0.1 (23A355). Source: the official restore IPSW with SHA-256 2773217713e94b81fbbaa6ecb6b7e87fb176f58f5edefdb868d8d71ec6547bd2.

Observed

  • The IPSW contains both kernelcache.release.iphone12b and kernelcache.research.iphone12b. These are two archive artifacts, not two observed running kernels.
  • After decompression, both parse as arm64e Mach-O FILESET images. Both report Darwin 25.0.0 and XNU 12377.2.9~1. Their Mach-O UUIDs differ: release FF7B4C89-4C36-6E92-9771-FB767E41C476; research F55B37F0-CAF2-BA23-7810-89585562057B.
  • Each fileset contains 239 LC_FILESET_ENTRY load commands. The ipsw kernel kexts --json parser returns 256 unique extension metadata records for each variant. These counts describe different structures and should not be treated as equal.
  • An extension record includes a bundle identifier, version, optional bundle path, and declared bundle dependencies. It is metadata parsed from the kernelcache; it does not establish that a standalone .kext file exists on the installed filesystem or that the extension is loaded at runtime.

Interpretation and next question

The restore package provides two kernelcache variants for the same target build. The research label is an IPSW archive filename, not evidence that this device booted it. To identify the running variant, compare a trustworthy on-device kernel identity with the published UUID and build metadata. To understand an individual extension's behavior, select its exact fileset image for focused static analysis and, when appropriate, confirm a hypothesis on the device.

Reproduce

The archive membership and hashes are in `firmware-archive.json` ↗; parsed kernel metadata is in `kernel.json` ↗. The exact extraction, decompression, and parser commands appear in the acquisition record ↗. Neither kernelcache binary is committed.
research.summary: The release and research artifacts share a build but have distinct Mach-O UUIDs. Fileset entries and kext metadata count different structures.

SpringBoard: from launchd declaration to cached framework

Target: iPhone 11 (iPhone12,1), iOS 26.0.1 (23A355). Static evidence comes from the official restore IPSW with SHA-256 2773217713e94b81fbbaa6ecb6b7e87fb176f58f5edefdb868d8d71ec6547bd2.

Observed chain

  1. The FileSystem image contains /System/Library/LaunchDaemons/com.apple.SpringBoard.plist (SHA-256 30a04d78624e2ec5274aacf1882470b030df1d3552a87fa37eac0428aaa19222). Its Label is com.apple.SpringBoard, its ProgramArguments[0] is /System/Library/CoreServices/SpringBoard.app/SpringBoard, its declared user is mobile, and it declares 39 Mach service names. The executable path also occurs as a regular file in the FileSystem catalog.
  2. That executable has SHA-256 188cef45c06b69dba1f4cbcfb30be85faa6d1c703638ae3ec3c3371f9a03c3f3. REA/Ghidra identifies its local entry at 0x100000568 as a thunk to _SBSystemAppMain, and that thunk points to an external _SBSystemAppMain imported from /System/Library/PrivateFrameworks/SpringBoard.framework/SpringBoard. REA Evidence: ev_2f476096cb74b7b891103bbaa5ecc26416371499ed5fccd47bcf85c60fb82dd9.
  3. The executable has LC_LOAD_DYLIB commands for SpringBoard.framework, Foundation, libobjc.A.dylib, and libSystem.B.dylib. REA Evidence: ev_4de480e295d07e8f769ab0d716989293f887c3253834445749a5db28e915ad38.
  4. The intact SystemOS arm64e dyld shared cache lists the SpringBoard.framework image at that logical install name, with UUID 8676BE2A-9484-3492-888E-7DE10333250F. None of the three mounted installed-system images has a standalone regular file at that path. ipsw dyld macho <MAIN_DSC> /System/Library/PrivateFrameworks/SpringBoard.framework/SpringBoard --symbols lists external _SBSystemAppMain at 0x21d604c60.
  5. The service Mach-O index ↗ records all four direct imports of the SpringBoard executable and matches each install name to an image in the same build's iOS shared cache. This is an exact static catalog match, not an observed runtime load.

Interpretation

The launchd plist, disk executable, and in-cache framework are three distinct objects. The disk executable is a small entry point that imports the framework function; the cache holds an image exporting that function. This is a concrete example of why locating only the on-disk app executable would miss the component code of interest.

The REA header-only dylib trace marks absolute system-library paths as outside-target, so it does not prove a live dyld resolution or that this job ran on the connected phone. The cache catalog independently establishes that the named framework image is present in this official build. The 39 Mach names are declarations, not observed IPC traffic.

Reproduce

The plist and its fields are in `launchd.json` ↗. The executable and framework-image paths are in `filesystem.json.gz` ↗ and `dyld.json` ↗. Follow the acquisition record ↗ to obtain the exact IPSW and cache. Open the mounted SpringBoard executable in REA with the Ghidra provider; run list_procedures and trace_dylib_resolution. Inspect the exact cache image with the ipsw dyld macho command above. The REA snapshot and Apple binaries remain local, outside Git.
research.summary: A stock launchd plist points to a disk executable whose entry thunk imports a SpringBoard.framework function present in the dyld shared cache.

SpringBoard lifecycle entry points in iOS 26.0.1

Target: iPhone 11 (iPhone12,1), build 23A355, iOS arm64e dyld cache UUID C0A7E671-35E1-3E6C-842D-FCE4E0A08C7E. The inspected framework is /System/Library/PrivateFrameworks/SpringBoard.framework/SpringBoard, Mach-O UUID 8676BE2A-9484-3492-888E-7DE10333250F.

Observed

  • The stock com.apple.SpringBoard launchd plist points to the small disk executable /System/Library/CoreServices/SpringBoard.app/SpringBoard. Its entry thunk imports _SBSystemAppMain from the cached SpringBoard.framework image, as traced in the launch-chain note ↗.
  • The intact cache exports _SBSystemAppMain at 0x21d604c60. A single-image extraction with ipsw dyld extract produced a local 96 MB analysis derivative, SHA-256 7732a59763b6fa34a52bfe8531d6dc0fcfa69761f6a96f438c0cda3363bb20be; its Mach-O UUID matches the cache image. The derivative is not a standalone file observed on the phone or in the mounted IPSW volumes.
  • ipsw class-dump on the intact cache reports SpringBoard as a subclass of UISystemShellApplication and lists UIApplicationDelegate among 16 adopted protocols. This selected class dump contains 645 method declarations (4 class, 641 instance) and 93 property declarations. These counts describe metadata in this image, not a runtime call trace.
  • The metadata names several startup-related entry points: +initializeSystemServicesBeforeApplicationDidFinishLaunching at 0x21d69fde4, -applicationDidFinishLaunching: at 0x21d6a1a48, -_completeStartupAfterMainSceneConnect: at 0x21d6a41d8, -_startBulletinBoardServer at 0x21d6a1730, -_startSystemStatusServerAndFriends at 0x21d6a38e4, and -_initializeDeferredItems at 0x21d6aafc8.
  • The class's declared instance variables include _mainWorkspace, _lockScreenService, _homeScreenService, _appSwitcherSystemService, _notificationDispatcher, and _restartManager. Their names and offsets are visible in the cache metadata; this observation alone does not establish when or how they are initialized.
  • The framework has 244 direct Mach-O dylib load declarations in the dependency catalog ↗. They describe potential load relationships, not calls from any particular startup method.
  • The image-wide method catalog ↗ records 52,025 method entries across 2,633 classes and 108 categories in this framework. This includes all 645 declarations on the SpringBoard class itself. Every recorded implementation address is inside this image's __TEXT segment. The site method view ↗ searches selectors and addresses; its coverage is limited to indexed cache images. See the method-surface note ↗ for scope and duplicate entries.

Interpretation and open questions

The static evidence separates three levels: launchd's program declaration, the disk executable's imported entry point, and lifecycle selectors implemented in the cached framework. The method names suggest useful places to investigate service setup, scene connection, and deferred startup. A selector name is only a lead: the call graph, branch conditions, initialization order, and actual device execution still need function-body analysis or bounded runtime observation. No tweak hook is recommended from names alone.

A focused LLVM disassembly now establishes selected direct calls, conditions, and the branch from _SBSystemAppMain to _UIApplicationMain; see the startup function note ↗. It does not establish the internal control flow of the lifecycle selectors listed above or which paths executed on the phone. Their function bodies and a bounded, read-only runtime trace remain follow-up work.

Reproduce

Use the exact IPSW and intact cache family identified in the acquisition record ↗. The following commands keep Apple binary material under the ignored .local directory:

ipsw dyld macho <MAIN_DSC> /System/Library/PrivateFrameworks/SpringBoard.framework/SpringBoard --symbols

ipsw class-dump <MAIN_DSC> /System/Library/PrivateFrameworks/SpringBoard.framework/SpringBoard --class '^SpringBoard$' --re -V

ipsw dyld extract <MAIN_DSC> /System/Library/PrivateFrameworks/SpringBoard.framework/SpringBoard --output .local/rea/extracted --slide --objc --stubs --cache <MAIN_DSC>.a2s

Save the complete class dump output under ignored .local/rea/springboard-all-classes.txt, then run the catalog command in the method-surface note ↗.

The full class dump, extracted binary, and disassembly remain local. Published metadata and this note are derived from the exact build; no live execution is asserted.
research.summary: The intact cache identifies SpringBoard's startup selectors, class relationships, and framework dependencies; function ordering remains to be verified.

What happens before SpringBoard enters UIKit?

Target: iPhone 11 (iPhone12,1), iOS 26.0.1 (23A355). Source: official restore IPSW SHA-256 2773217713e94b81fbbaa6ecb6b7e87fb176f58f5edefdb868d8d71ec6547bd2, SystemOS arm64e dyld cache family UUID C0A7E671-35E1-3E6C-842D-FCE4E0A08C7E. This note inspects _SBSystemAppMain in the cache's /System/Library/PrivateFrameworks/SpringBoard.framework/SpringBoard image, Mach-O UUID 8676BE2A-9484-3492-888E-7DE10333250F.

The framework was extracted for local analysis with ipsw dyld extract. That 96 MB derivative has SHA-256 7732a59763b6fa34a52bfe8531d6dc0fcfa69761f6a96f438c0cda3363bb20be. It is not a standalone file observed on the phone or in a mounted installed-system image. The launch-chain note ↗ identifies the preceding launchd declaration and disk executable.

Observed instructions

_SBSystemAppMain begins at 0x21d604c60 in this extracted image. These instruction addresses and call targets were checked with `verify_springboard_startup.py` ↗, using Apple's llvm-objdump, llvm-nm, and dwarfdump from xcrun.

  • 0x21d604c88–0x21d604c8c: Saves incoming x1 and w0 to stack slots, later reloaded as argv and argc by the usual arm64 calling convention.
  • 0x21d605c20: Branches past a version-comparison block when x19 is zero.
  • 0x21d605c30–0x21d605c5c: Calls compareBuildVersion:withPrecision:; a conditional branch can bypass deleteAllSystemSnapshots and _setClearSystemAppSnapshotsWhenLoaded:. These calls are present in the code, not proven to run on every start.
  • 0x21d605c70–0x21d605cb4: Two compareBuildVersionString:withPrecision: calls each have a branch around _setClearAllLegacySnapshotsWhenLoaded:.
  • 0x21d605cd8: Calls migrateAndRemoveOldDefaults.
  • 0x21d605d2c, 0x21d605ec4: Contains calls to setLastSystemBuildVersion: and setLastRestoreIdentifier: later in the function. Their runtime paths require further tracing.
  • 0x21d606054–0x21d606064: Calls removeAllImagesWithCompletion: on a session cache, then earlyInitialization.
  • 0x21d6060f8–0x21d606104: Reloads saved argc into w0 and argv into x1, then branches to 0x2225247a0. The extracted image's symbol table names that exact target _UIApplicationMain.

Interpretation and limits

The direct static path reaches UIKit's _UIApplicationMain after SpringBoard-specific setup and migration instructions. The conditional version and snapshot calls suggest different startup behavior according to stored state. This is a statement about the code in this exact build: no device trace establishes which branches the connected phone took, whether snapshot deletion occurred, or how long initialization took. The calls' side effects also cannot be established from selector names alone.

The branch target is an imported address in the extracted derivative. The symbol match identifies the target, but this analysis does not inspect UIKit's implementation or prove live dyld binding. The x2/x3 values passed to _UIApplicationMain have not been resolved here. SpringBoard's later application delegate and scene lifecycle methods remain separate questions in the lifecycle note ↗. This analysis is not yet enough to choose a reliable tweak hook.

Reproduce

Follow the acquisition record ↗ to obtain and verify the exact IPSW and intact cache. Extract only the SpringBoard.framework image into ignored .local storage as shown in the lifecycle note ↗, then run:

python3 tools/verify_springboard_startup.py .local/rea/extracted/SpringBoard

The script refuses a different SHA-256 or Mach-O UUID, verifies 19 address-specific instructions, and checks that the direct branch target is named _UIApplicationMain. Apple binaries and full disassembly remain local; this note publishes only derived observations.
research.summary: Selected instructions in the exact cache image show conditional build and snapshot handling, early initialization, and a direct branch from SBSystemAppMain to UIApplicationMain.

How much of SpringBoard.framework's Objective-C method surface is indexed?

Target: iPhone 11 (iPhone12,1), iOS 26.0.1 (23A355). Source: official restore IPSW SHA-256 2773217713e94b81fbbaa6ecb6b7e87fb176f58f5edefdb868d8d71ec6547bd2, iOS arm64e dyld cache family UUID C0A7E671-35E1-3E6C-842D-FCE4E0A08C7E. The inspected image is /System/Library/PrivateFrameworks/SpringBoard.framework/SpringBoard, Mach-O UUID 8676BE2A-9484-3492-888E-7DE10333250F.

Observed coverage

  • A complete ipsw class-dump --re -V of that cache image reports 2,633 class declarations, 108 categories, and 1,317 protocol declarations. The full local dump has SHA-256 43494a07674ac0462bc1241f9f5896111a8d53d7bc8d7de9271a301d47222725; it is not published.
  • The derived method catalog ↗ contains 52,025 method entries: 51,636 under classes and 389 under categories. Every entry has a selector, class or category label, and implementation address inside this exact image's __TEXT segment. The SpringBoard class contributes 645 of these entries.
  • All 2,633 class names and metadata addresses match the separate dyld Objective-C optimization table ↗ for this image. All 108 category metadata addresses are within this image's mapped segments. The class dump's own table-of-contents counts match the parsed class, category, and protocol declaration counts.
  • Five class method sets contain a selector repeated with two different implementation addresses. Both entries are preserved. This static dump does not establish which one wins at runtime.
  • The 1,317 protocol declarations are excluded from the implementation-address count. A protocol's method declaration is a requirement or optional interface, not an implementation in this image.

How to use it

The Objective-C methods view ↗ lists indexed images and searches class names there. Choose SpringBoard.framework to search its class names, category labels, selectors, and implementation addresses. For example, SpringBoard's own methods ↗ show applicationDidFinishLaunching: at 0x21d6a1a48. The class table ↗ links its exact SpringBoard entry to that filtered list. This supports targeted reverse engineering and candidate discovery; selecting a tweak hook still requires function-body and runtime evidence.

The count above is for one cache image in one build. The site separately indexes method results for all 4,170 iOS cache images ↗, including explicit empty results. Static class dumps do not establish dynamically added methods, generated runtime subclasses, or methods whose metadata is unavailable to the tool. A selector name or IMP address does not prove a method was called on the connected phone.

Reproduce

Follow the acquisition record ↗ to obtain the exact IPSW and intact cache family. Keep the full class dump and extracted analysis derivative under ignored .local storage:

ipsw class-dump <MAIN_DSC> /System/Library/PrivateFrameworks/SpringBoard.framework/SpringBoard --re -V --no-color > .local/rea/springboard-all-classes.txt

ipsw dyld extract <MAIN_DSC> /System/Library/PrivateFrameworks/SpringBoard.framework/SpringBoard --output .local/rea/extracted --slide --objc --stubs --cache <MAIN_DSC>.a2s

python3 tools/catalog_objc_image_methods.py --class-dump .local/rea/springboard-all-classes.txt --image .local/rea/extracted/SpringBoard --image-sha256 7732a59763b6fa34a52bfe8531d6dc0fcfa69761f6a96f438c0cda3363bb20be --install-name /System/Library/PrivateFrameworks/SpringBoard.framework/SpringBoard --segments catalog/ios/23A355/dyld-segments.json --objc-classes catalog/ios/23A355/objc-classes.json --expected-method-count 52025 --output catalog/ios/23A355/objc-image-methods-SpringBoard.json.gz

The generator checks the derivative SHA-256 and UUID, source-build identities, class-table equality, declaration counts, and every implementation address. The website builder repeats the catalog consistency and address checks before publishing derived metadata.
research.summary: An exact-cache class dump yields 52,025 Objective-C method entries across 2,633 classes and 108 categories, with all IMP addresses checked against the image's code segment.

What does SpringBoard set up after UIKit calls its launch delegate?

Target: iPhone 11 (iPhone12,1), iOS 26.0.1 (23A355), SystemOS arm64e dyld cache UUID C0A7E671-35E1-3E6C-842D-FCE4E0A08C7E. The inspected image is /System/Library/PrivateFrameworks/SpringBoard.framework/SpringBoard, Mach-O UUID 8676BE2A-9484-3492-888E-7DE10333250F. Its local ipsw dyld extract derivative has SHA-256 7732a59763b6fa34a52bfe8531d6dc0fcfa69761f6a96f438c0cda3363bb20be; the binary is not published.

The launch-chain note ↗ follows launchd to the small disk executable, and the startup note ↗ follows _SBSystemAppMain to UIKit's UIApplicationMain. This note inspects one later function, -[SpringBoard applicationDidFinishLaunching:] at 0x21d6a1a48, in the exact extracted image. It is a bounded static reading, not a device execution trace.

Direct instruction evidence

  • At 0x21d6a1b20, the method directly calls _SBCommonInitialize.
  • At 0x21d6a1cf4, it sends checkInPorts to a receiver whose identity is not established by this instruction alone.
  • At 0x21d6a1eac–0x21d6a1ec4, it reloads one receiver and consecutively sends _startSystemStatusServerAndFriends, _prepareBacklightServices, and _setUpHUDControllerAndFriends. The register setup establishes the common receiver at these three call sites; the selector names do not establish the called methods' effects.
  • At 0x21d6a1fd0–0x21d6a1fdc, it obtains a sharedInstance and sends completeStartup to that returned object. The class of that object is not resolved here.
  • Later call sites include initWithWindowSceneManager: at 0x21d6a2d08, initWithStartupOrientation: at 0x21d6a31c0, and initWithDisplayManager:sceneManagerCoordinator:assertionCoordinator:powerLogReporter: at 0x21d6a330c. These are evidence of setup-oriented messages, not proof of which objects are constructed or which scene becomes visible.

The method also contains startup signpost literals including SB_STARTUP_COMMON_INIT, SB_STARTUP_USER_SESSION_CONTROLLER, and SB_STARTUP_SERVICES. The sequence of instruction addresses gives code layout and local call order. Branches, callbacks, and errors can change actual execution order; no duration or successful completion is inferred from these names.

The framework has 52,025 indexed Objective-C method entries ↗ and 244 direct Mach-O load declarations. Its declared loads include UIKit, FrontBoardServices, BackBoardServices, Foundation, and CoreFoundation. UIKit itself re-exports UIKitCore in the exact dependency catalog ↗. These declarations connect the layers statically; they do not prove live loading or a safe tweak hook.

Reproduce and limits

Use the exact cache identified in the acquisition record ↗, extract this image into ignored .local storage, verify the SHA-256 and UUID above, then run:

xcrun llvm-objdump -m -d --dis-symname '-[SpringBoard applicationDidFinishLaunching:]' .local/rea/extracted/SpringBoard

The selected instruction addresses above are in that output. A REA/Ghidra attempt to analyze this 96 MB image did not finish within the tool's five-minute call limit; this note makes no decompiler claim. The receivers and effects of selected messages, the full control-flow graph, actual runtime path, and hook safety remain unverified.
research.summary: Selected exact-image instructions in applicationDidFinishLaunching: call common initialization, send system-status, backlight, and HUD setup messages, and expose later scene-related construction sites; runtime effects remain unknown.

How does a SpringBoard window scene reach startup completion code?

Target: iPhone 11 (iPhone12,1), iOS 26.0.1 (23A355), SystemOS arm64e cache UUID C0A7E671-35E1-3E6C-842D-FCE4E0A08C7E. All instruction addresses below come from the cached /System/Library/PrivateFrameworks/SpringBoard.framework/SpringBoard image (UUID 8676BE2A-9484-3492-888E-7DE10333250F), extracted locally with ipsw dyld extract (SHA-256 7732a59763b6fa34a52bfe8531d6dc0fcfa69761f6a96f438c0cda3363bb20be). The executable bytes are not published.

Apple documents the scene-delegate connection callback ↗. The classes below are private SpringBoard classes, so the public documentation supplies context for the callback shape, not proof of their internal behavior.

Observed static path

  1. SBEmbeddedDisplayWindowSceneDelegate is a subclass of SBAbstractWindowSceneDelegate in the exact class dump. Its scene:willConnectToSession:options: implementation starts at 0x21dcf46a4, calls objc_msgSendSuper2 at 0x21dcf4730, and sends noteMainSceneConnected: at 0x21dcf4798 after a role comparison. The superclass implementation at 0x21d7976dc conditionally sends _commonSceneSetupForScene: at 0x21d797814.
  2. The superclass's _commonSceneSetupForScene: at 0x21d798978 sends _configureForConnectingWindowScene:windowSceneContext: at 0x21d7989d0. The embedded delegate overrides that selector at 0x21dcf3b48. Objective-C dispatch makes this a candidate connection between the two bodies; no runtime receiver trace proves the override was chosen on the phone.
  3. The embedded delegate's configuration body constructs a block whose invoke address is 0x21dcf3f20 (0x21dcf3e4c–0x21dcf3e60) and passes it to objc_retainBlock at 0x21dcf3e8c. The retained block is stored through an instance-field offset at 0x21dcf3e98–0x21dcf3e9c. The exact later caller of this block is not established here.
  4. At the start of the block, a weakly held object is loaded and checked; a null result branches away at 0x21dcf3f50. Otherwise, at 0x21dcf3f68, the block sends _completeStartupAfterMainSceneConnect: to a global object and passes a captured window scene as its argument. The SpringBoard class implements that selector at 0x21d6a41d8; dynamic dispatch to that particular IMP is not proven by the selector name alone.
  5. Within that 5,770-line implementation, selected call sites show a dataRecoveryRequired check (0x21d6a43b0) whose false branch skips performDataRecovery (0x21d6a4420), followed later in code by setWindowScene: (0x21d6a44f8), _startBulletinBoardServer (0x21d6a7b28), and setHasFinishedLaunching: (0x21d6a8818). These are bounded instruction observations, not a complete control-flow or side-effect analysis.

Separately, SBEmbeddedScenesConnectionManager implements noteMainSceneConnected: at 0x21d8231b4; it stores a scene reference and sends _reevaluateSceneConnection at 0x21d8232b4. Its reevaluation body includes a completeStartupAfterAllEmbeddedScenesConnect send at 0x21d82377c behind conditional branches. The relationship between this manager path and the retained configuration block needs a focused callback/ownership trace before a single execution timeline can be claimed.

Boundary and reproduction

The code establishes a superclass setup call, an override with a retained block, and the block's candidate SpringBoard startup-completion send. It does not establish the block's invocation timing, which scene role was present, whether data recovery ran, or the connected device's runtime path. No tweak hook is selected.

Verify the image SHA-256 and UUID above, then disassemble the named functions with xcrun llvm-objdump -m -d --dis-symname '<symbol>' .local/rea/extracted/SpringBoard. The symbols are -[SBEmbeddedDisplayWindowSceneDelegate scene:willConnectToSession:options:], -[SBAbstractWindowSceneDelegate scene:willConnectToSession:options:], -[SBAbstractWindowSceneDelegate _commonSceneSetupForScene:], -[SBEmbeddedDisplayWindowSceneDelegate _configureForConnectingWindowScene:windowSceneContext:], ___94-[SBEmbeddedDisplayWindowSceneDelegate _configureForConnectingWindowScene:windowSceneContext:]_block_invoke, and -[SpringBoard _completeStartupAfterMainSceneConnect:]. The earlier startup note ↗ covers the application launch callback before this scene-specific path.
research.summary: Exact-image instructions link the embedded scene delegate's connection callback to superclass setup, a retained configuration block, and a candidate SpringBoard startup-completion send. Block invocation timing and runtime dispatch remain unknown.

How does this UIKitCore image enter the application event cycle?

What does UIApplication _run install before entering the event loop?

Target: iPhone 11 (iPhone12,1), iOS 26.0.1 (23A355), SystemOS arm64e cache UUID C0A7E671-35E1-3E6C-842D-FCE4E0A08C7E. The inspected /System/Library/PrivateFrameworks/UIKitCore.framework/UIKitCore image has UUID C98EAB32-B273-3430-B0C5-46522C904CBB. The locally extracted analysis derivative has SHA-256 fa0602d08391372c60d63aac6e3af356c14b95da25674e28e014489b749ad112; the binary is not published.

The entry note ↗ establishes an _run message from UIApplicationMain. The exact class dump lists -[UIApplication _run] at 0x188a1cac4, and the extracted image contains the matching function body.

Direct instruction evidence

  • The first portion sends a series of registration messages, including user-default, time, language, locale, key-bag, and keyboard-layout notifications (0x188a1cb50–0x188a1cba0). These call sites do not show which notifications were posted on the connected phone.
  • At 0x188a1cc80, _run calls the imported CFRunLoopGetMain. At 0x188a1cc8c, it passes that result to -[UIEventDispatcher _installEventRunLoopSources:].
  • -[UIEventDispatcher _installEventRunLoopSources:] begins at 0x189d92d90 and returns immediately for a null receiver. For the non-null path, it calls imported CFRunLoopSourceCreate at 0x189d92e18 and 0x189d92e64, then CFRunLoopAddSource at 0x189d92e38 and 0x189d92e78. The first source creation is bypassed when _UIUpdateCycleEnabled returns true (0x189d92de4–0x189d92df8); the second remains in the shown path. Apple's API reference ↗ explains what adding a source means in public CoreFoundation terms.
  • _run has a conditional system-app/FrontBoard path that can send _runWithMainScene:transitionContext:completion: (0x188a1ccf4–0x188a1cd40), plus other branches for a system UI service or extension behavior. These branches prevent treating the method as one linear startup sequence.
  • At 0x188a1cdd8, _run calls imported GSEventRun. The exact UIKitCore image declares a direct load of GraphicsServices; the next note ↗ follows that symbol into the cached GraphicsServices image and its CFRunLoopRunInMode call.

This establishes a static bridge from UIKitCore's application runner to CoreFoundation run-loop source setup and GraphicsServices event running. It does not establish which startup branch executed, the identity of every callback attached to the sources, the live run-loop mode, event delivery order, or hook safety.

Does GraphicsServices enter CoreFoundation's run loop?

Target: iPhone 11 (iPhone12,1), iOS 26.0.1 (23A355), SystemOS arm64e cache UUID C0A7E671-35E1-3E6C-842D-FCE4E0A08C7E. The inspected /System/Library/PrivateFrameworks/GraphicsServices.framework/GraphicsServices image has UUID 4EB73F50-CDF2-3161-94C0-0F3E7002B67C. Its local ipsw dyld extract derivative has SHA-256 fa9e9a556605ea732487ebb840986962cef09f6cbf503c48ba50d764d919ee62; the binary is not published.

The UIKitCore `_run` note ↗ identifies an imported GSEventRun call. The exact dependency catalog ↗ records a UIKitCore load of GraphicsServices and a GraphicsServices load of CoreFoundation. Those declarations align with, but do not replace, the instruction evidence below.

Direct instruction evidence

  • _GSEventRun at 0x22246e19c sets w0 to zero and branches to _GSEventRunModal at 0x22246e1a0.
  • _GSEventRunModal begins at 0x22246e420. In its loop it obtains a value from an array through imported CFArrayGetValueAtIndex (0x22246e484), checks for null (0x22246e488), then calls imported CFRunLoopRunInMode at 0x22246e494. The immediately preceding instruction sets w1 to zero (0x22246e490). Apple documents ↗ that this argument is returnAfterSourceHandled; the code supplies false at this site. A follow-up note ↗ traces the mode argument to the last entry of a mutable array, but does not identify its runtime value. The duration literal is not decoded here.
  • A conditional branch at 0x22246e498 can repeat the loop. A null mode leads to a logging path. This does not prove the number of iterations or which modes the phone used.
  • The imported CFRunLoopRunInMode stub at 0x2225af230 is identified by the derivative symbol table. The CoreFoundation note ↗ follows its implementation at 0x1830a3018 to CFRunLoopGetCurrent and __CFRunLoopRunSpecificWithOptions.

The resulting static call chain is UIApplicationMain → UIApplication _run → GSEventRun → GSEventRunModal → CFRunLoopRunInMode → CoreFoundation's internal run function. Import names, load declarations, and exact-image implementations support this path. Runtime binding, actual branch choices, callback execution, and event semantics on the connected phone remain unverified.

Where does GraphicsServices get the mode passed to CFRunLoopRunInMode?

Target: iPhone 11 (iPhone12,1), iOS 26.0.1 (23A355), SystemOS arm64e cache UUID C0A7E671-35E1-3E6C-842D-FCE4E0A08C7E. The inspected /System/Library/PrivateFrameworks/GraphicsServices.framework/GraphicsServices image has UUID 4EB73F50-CDF2-3161-94C0-0F3E7002B67C. Its local ipsw dyld extract derivative has SHA-256 fa9e9a556605ea732487ebb840986962cef09f6cbf503c48ba50d764d919ee62; the binary is not published.

The event-runner note ↗ follows GSEventRun into GSEventRunModal and then CFRunLoopRunInMode. This note checks the mode value's immediate source and the two named functions that change it. It is a static reading of this exact cache image, not a device execution trace.

Direct instruction evidence

  • _GSEventRunModal begins at 0x22246e420. At 0x22246e45c–0x22246e484, it loads a shared pointer at image-data offset 0x468, calls CFArrayGetCount, subtracts one, and calls CFArrayGetValueAtIndex on the same array. After a null check, it passes the returned value in x0 to CFRunLoopRunInMode at 0x22246e494. Thus the mode argument comes from the last entry of that array at this call site. The code does not identify which concrete mode string occupies the last entry at runtime.
  • _GSEventPushRunLoopMode at 0x222470094 loads the same array pointer (0x2224700ac). When it is null, the function calls CFArrayCreateMutable at 0x2224700c0 and stores the result at the shared offset (0x2224700c4). It passes the incoming x0 value to CFArrayAppendValue at 0x2224700cc. These instructions establish a last-in selection mechanism for later modal-loop iterations.
  • _GSEventPopRunLoopMode at 0x2224700f4 loads the same array pointer (0x22247010c). If it is non-null, it obtains the last value with CFArrayGetCount and CFArrayGetValueAtIndex (0x22247011c–0x222470128). It compares that value with its incoming argument using CFStringCompare with zero options (0x22247013c). Only a zero comparison result reaches CFArrayRemoveValueAtIndex at 0x222470158. Apple's array API ↗ defines removal by index; these instructions select the final index.
  • Both push and pop load a separately stored run-loop pointer at shared offset 0x470 and tail-call CFRunLoopStop (0x2224700d4–0x2224700f0, 0x22247015c–0x222470180). Apple documents ↗ that stopping a run loop returns control from its current activation. GSEventRunModal has a branch back to its array lookup after CFRunLoopRunInMode returns (0x22246e498–0x22246e49c), allowing a subsequent iteration to read the changed last entry. This is a possible static control path; the exact activation and scheduling on the phone are unverified.
  • __GSEventInitializeShared stores CFRunLoopGetCurrent at the same 0x470 offset on its no-queue branch (0x22246df50–0x22246df54). The other initialization branch is not traced to an equivalent assignment here, so this note does not claim the stored run-loop pointer is always set.

The array is used like a mode stack in these three function bodies. This does not identify the original mode pushed by a caller, prove balanced push/pop calls, show which process owns a caller, or establish that a particular mode ran on the connected device. No tweak hook is selected.

Reproduce

Verify the derivative SHA-256 and image UUID above, then disassemble _GSEventRunModal, _GSEventPushRunLoopMode, _GSEventPopRunLoopMode, and __GSEventInitializeShared with xcrun llvm-objdump -m -d --dis-symname '<symbol>' .local/rea/extracted/GraphicsServices. Imported function names were cross-checked with xcrun llvm-nm -n on the same derivative. The Apple binary and full disassembly stay local.

Apple's CFRunLoop documentation ↗ describes a thread's run loop, its sources, timers, observers, and modes. This note checks the entry wrappers in the exact cached image. Exact-image observations

  • _CFRunLoopRun starts at 0x1831213ec. It calls _CFRunLoopGetCurrent at 0x183121418 and __CFRunLoopRunSpecificWithOptions at 0x183121428. After inspecting the result and process-state flags, a conditional branch at 0x183121450 can return to the GetCurrent call. These instructions show an entry wrapper and a possible repeated invocation, without establishing which result values occurred at runtime.
  • _CFRunLoopRunInMode starts at 0x1830a3018. It retains incoming mode and duration arguments, calls _CFRunLoopGetCurrent at 0x1830a3058, then branches to __CFRunLoopRunSpecificWithOptions at 0x1830a308c. This is a code-path observation, not a complete reading of the internal scheduler.
  • The named-symbol catalog ↗ records 7,977 unique named __text rows, including these entry points and the internal __CFRunLoopRunSpecificWithOptions. The Objective-C catalog ↗ separately records 2,395 methods across 141 classes and three categories. These counts overlap where names refer to the same code and do not enumerate all C functions.
  • The dependency catalog ↗ records five direct loads for CoreFoundation, including an upward Foundation load and a libobjc.A.dylib re-export. Foundation declares a CoreFoundation re-export. These are static load commands, not observed runtime bindings.

The wrappers make CoreFoundation a useful next stop for studying event and timer scheduling, but this pass does not decompile __CFRunLoopRunSpecificWithOptions, identify the active mode on the phone, prove that the static UIKit path executed, or establish a hook point.

Reading Foundation's static dependency reach

Target: iPhone 11 (iPhone12,1), iOS 26.0.1 (23A355). The source is the official IPSW with SHA-256 2773217713e94b81fbbaa6ecb6b7e87fb176f58f5edefdb868d8d71ec6547bd2, iOS cache UUID C0A7E671-35E1-3E6C-842D-FCE4E0A08C7E.

Observed paths

  • The cached Foundation image (/System/Library/Frameworks/Foundation.framework/Foundation, UUID 0555AF54-2075-3F2D-BC40-733E55EEE95A) declares 29 direct Mach-O dylib loads, including two LC_LOAD_WEAK_DYLIB commands.
  • Following only exact in-cache install-name matches and excluding weak commands reaches 123 other images. Including weak commands at every step reaches 1,353. The count excludes Foundation itself. These are graph reachability counts, not images observed in one process.
  • One two-step chain without weak loads is Foundation LC_LOAD_DYLIB → CFNetwork LC_LOAD_DYLIB → /usr/lib/libsqlite3.dylib. Both edges occur in the direct-load catalog ↗.
  • One direct weak edge is Foundation LC_LOAD_WEAK_DYLIB → /System/Library/PrivateFrameworks/CoreAutoLayout.framework/CoreAutoLayout. It appears in the interactive dependency view ↗ only when weak loads are included.

Interpretation

The large difference between 123 and 1,353 illustrates how optional edges can expand a transitive static graph. A shortest path answers which declared chain connects these cached install names under the selected edge rule. It does not establish that dyld followed the chain, that a weak target resolved, that Foundation called the target's code, or that all reachable images were loaded in one process. Other paths to the same image can exist; the website displays one shortest chain.

Reproduce

The dependency catalog ↗ records every image UUID and its direct load commands. The graph logic ↗ performs breadth-first search, ignores nonmatching install names, and guards against cycles. node tools/test_reach.mjs checks cycle, weak-load, unmatched-target, and shortest-path behavior on a small graph. The website computes reachability from the validated catalog in the browser; no extracted Apple binary is published.
research.summary: An exact-cache graph links Foundation to 123 images without weak loads and 1,353 when weak declarations are included.
